chunks: Ways to raise a clock frequency (PLL). The question: What can you use increase clock frequency?
A PLL (phase-locked loop) is a circuit that makes a fast clock out of a slow, accurate one. You start with a cheap, stable reference such as a crystal.
The PLL multiplies its frequency by a number you choose, usually a whole number. It is used because crystals can't directly make very high frequencies cheaply and accurately.
Imagine a slow drummer keeping perfect time, and a fast drummer who plays 40 beats for each of the slow drummer's beats.
The fast drummer listens to the slow one and nudges the pace so that every 40th beat lands exactly on the slow drummer's beat.
The fast drummer is as steady as the slow one, just 40 times faster. The picture breaks down in that a real PLL adds a little timing wobble of its own.
The VCO output is divided by N and compared with the reference.
When they match, f out over N equals f ref , so the output is exactly N times the crystal frequency, with the crystal's long-term accuracy.
Reference clock: the slow, stable source, usually a crystal. VCO: voltage-controlled oscillator, the fast oscillator whose speed is set by a control voltage.
Divider: a counter that divides a frequency by N . Jitter: tiny cycle-to-cycle timing errors in a clock. PLL: the whole loop. How it works is on "How a PLL works".
Start with a 25 megahertz crystal and a divide-by-40 in the feedback path.
The loop forces the divided VCO clock to match 25 megahertz, so the VCO itself must run at 25 times 40 equals 1000 megahertz, which is 1 gigahertz.
Change N to 20 and you get 500 megahertz from the same crystal. That is the whole idea.
"A PLL, used as a frequency multiplier. A stable low-frequency reference like a crystal feeds a loop containing a VCO and a divide-by-N in the feedback path.
The loop locks the divided VCO to the reference, so the output is N times the reference: 25 megahertz times 40 gives 1 gigahertz.
It's preferred over a very high-frequency crystal because it's flexible and the reference is clean and cheap.
Simpler options exist, like an XOR-based doubler or a higher-frequency oscillator, but a faster clock costs power, timing margin and jitter."
